(4) LOCAL GOVERNMENT FISCAL COLLAPSE — land revenue down ~65% from its 2020 peak and running at under a third of the 2021 level, producing public-sector wage arrears, unpaid contractor bills that cascade to construction workers, aggressive tax and fine enforcement on businesses, and the LGFV debt overhang. (5) LABOUR DISPLACEMENT — construction's share of migrant employment fell to the lowest since 2008; millions of low-skilled men displaced into delivery and ride-hailing, feeding the gig-economy oversupply and its wage deflation. (6) DEMOGRAPHIC DAMAGE — the housing-marriage nexus (83% of rural respondents believing a city apartment is a marriage prerequisite; mortgage-to-income rising from 16.2% to 57.4% between 2004 and 2021) contributed to marriages falling from 13.47 million couples in 2013 to 8.14 million in 2020 and 4.74 million in the first three quarters of 2024. Research indicates these deferred-marriage and deferred-birth behaviours become normalised, meaning the birth rate may not recover even if housing becomes affordable — the damage is permanent. (7) EDUCATIONAL AND CAREER DESTRUCTION — an entire cohort of civil engineering and architecture graduates entered a market that had lost half its jobs; the 46% five-year fall in graduates entering construction engineering is the largest among 46 occupational categories. (8) TRUST AND SOCIAL CONTRACT — the implicit promise that property always rises, which underwrote household compliance with a low-consumption high-savings model, has been broken; the resulting precautionary saving and deflationary psychology is now Beijing's central macroeconomic problem. (9) GHOST CITIES AND WASTED CAPITAL — years of construction with diminishing returns left tier-3/4 cities with stock they will never populate, an irreversible misallocation of an entire generation's savings.
risiko_sosial_indonesia: (1) A STRANDED-BUYER CRISIS AT SCALE — the clearest and most imminent risk. Indonesia runs pre-sale without mandatory escrow, and SEMA 3/2023 has removed buyers' bankruptcy leverage. LRT City's ~2,400 stranded buyers being chased by debt collectors for loans on undelivered apartments is a direct rehearsal of China's 2022 mortgage boycott, at 1/1000th of the scale. If the 3-million-homes push draws in undercapitalised developers under volume pressure, Indonesia could produce tens of thousands of such cases within three years — with no fiscal capacity for a 保交楼-scale rescue. (2) PERMANENT GENERATIONAL EXCLUSION AND ITS DEMOGRAPHIC ECHO — 51% of Gen Z already say they cannot afford a house; inheritance is the dominant acquisition route; Deloitte finds marriage and home purchase both being deferred. China's experience shows this hardens into a norm that does not reverse when affordability improves. Indonesia is running this risk while still inside its demographic bonus window, which is the worst possible timing: deferred household formation now compounds the fertility decline that will define Indonesia's 2050s. (3) ENTRENCHMENT OF INHERITED WEALTH — if ownership passes mainly by inheritance, property becomes the mechanism that freezes the Indonesian class structure, converting an aspirational middle class into a rentier/excluded binary. This is more socially corrosive in Indonesia than in China because Indonesian inequality is already higher and land ownership more concentrated. (4) PREDATORY SUBSTITUTE CREDIT — households locked out of KPR turn to paylater, pinjol, and multiguna loans at far higher rates; the affordability crisis converts into an unsecured-debt crisis among exactly the households least able to bear it. (5) SPECULATIVE LAND FRAUD — kavling and 'properti syariah' Ponzi schemes proliferate precisely when ownership is unattainable and yields are promised at 30-50%; OJK has recorded hundreds of illegal entities in the property and land sector. Victims are typically lower-middle-class savers with no recourse. (6) FOREIGN-PARENT CONTAGION — Indonesian buyers already hold units in projects by Country Garden (a defaulted Chinese developer) and CFLD (which stalled its Tangerang projects from 2018). Without ring-fencing rules, an offshore parent's collapse strands Indonesian households. (7) STRANDED STATE INFRASTRUCTURE — an under-populated IKN, or Mandalika/coastal estates built ahead of demand, is the Indonesian ghost-city risk, with the added feature that the losses land on the state budget rather than on private developers. (8) DISPLACEMENT AND LAND CONFLICT — the PSN mechanism used for private mega-estates (PIK 2 sea fences, land acquisition disputes) risks reproducing China's demolition-and-relocation conflicts without China's compensation capacity, in a democracy where such conflicts are electorally explosive. (9) CONSTRUCTION LABOUR PRECARITY — 8.7 million construction workers, overwhelmingly informal, with no unemployment insurance; a project-finance freeze transmits to household income within weeks.
unintended_consequences:
IN CHINA: (a) The three red lines, designed to prevent a crisis, precipitated it — a textbook case of correct diagnosis destroyed by wrong sequencing. (b) Administrative price-drop bans (限跌令) on new homes pushed price discovery entirely into the resale market, which then fell harder and faster, inverting the normal relationship where new homes trade at a premium and creating the bizarre situation of new-build prices holding while identical second-hand units nearby fell 30-40%. (c) 保交楼 succeeded at completing 7.5 million homes but, by adding finished supply into a falling market, accelerated the price decline it was partly meant to arrest. (d) The property crash pushed millions of displaced construction workers into food delivery and ride-hailing, creating the gig-labour glut and wage deflation that is now a separate policy problem. (e) The wealth destruction converted a high-savings, high-investment economy into a deflationary one, making the property crisis the proximate cause of China's consumption downgrade, youth unemployment and export-dependence — all of which then generated trade conflicts abroad. (f) Excess construction capacity and materials overcapacity are now being exported, deflating global building-materials prices and threatening manufacturers in importing countries including Indonesia. (g) The shelving of the property tax in 2022 left local governments with no replacement for land revenue and no politically feasible path to create one — a permanent fiscal wound caused by a temporary market condition. (h) Falling home prices did not improve fertility; the deferral behaviours had already become normalised, so the demographic damage outlived its cause.

PREDICTED FOR INDONESIA: (a) 0% down-payment/100% LTV policy, maintained for years to stimulate demand, maximises the number of buyers with no equity buffer — if any correction occurs, Indonesia will have manufactured its own negative-equity cohort using a policy meant to expand access. (b) SEMA 3/2023, intended to protect housing supply by preventing opportunistic bankruptcy petitions, has instead removed the main deterrent against developers taking buyer money and not delivering — protecting the supply side by disarming the demand side. (c) The 3-million-homes volume target, if pursued through quota pressure, will select for developers willing to promise cheaply rather than build reliably, manufacturing exactly the stalled-project problem it is meant to solve. (d) PPN DTP and other demand subsidies in a supply-constrained market are largely capitalised into land prices, transferring public money to landowners rather than to buyers. (e) Subsidised housing built where land is cheap — far from jobs and transit — creates remote unsold or abandoned estates, Indonesia's low-income version of China's tier-3 glut, and locks poor households into high commuting costs. (f) Tapera's mandatory 3% deduction, intended to fund housing, functions as a regressive payroll tax on workers who will never qualify for the housing it funds, and its funds' allocation to government bonds rather than housing has already drawn analyst criticism. (g) Chinese materials deflation lowers construction costs — good for affordability, bad for Indonesian building-materials employment — an unintended industrial-policy collision.
kelompok_rentan: (1) URBAN GEN Z AND YOUNGER MILLENNIALS WITHOUT PROPERTY-OWNING PARENTS — the single most affected group; 51% of Gen Z and 40% of millennials already report inability to buy, only 10% obtained a KPR, and inheritance is the dominant route, meaning those without inheritable property face permanent exclusion. (2) INFORMAL AND GIG WORKERS (>55% of the workforce, plus ~4-5 million platform drivers and couriers) — structurally unbankable for a KPR regardless of actual income; excluded from FLPP by documentation requirements; simultaneously the group most exposed to construction-sector job losses. (3) BUYERS OF UNFINISHED PRE-SOLD UNITS — the LRT City and Meikarta cohorts: households servicing KPA instalments and being pursued by debt collectors for assets that do not exist, with SEMA 3/2023 blocking their strongest legal remedy. This group faces total loss of a lifetime's savings. (4) LOW-INCOME (MBR) HOUSEHOLDS — 83.3% of the 9.9-15 million unit backlog, dependent on an FLPP programme that delivered only 22.15% of quota by mid-2026, and on remote subsidised estates with poor jobs access. (5) CONSTRUCTION WORKERS — 8.7 million people, overwhelmingly informal, without unemployment insurance, whose incomes stop within weeks of a project-finance freeze; disproportionately migrant, male, low-education, and supporting rural households through remittances. (6) SMALL SAVERS TARGETED BY LAND AND SYARIAH-PROPERTY SCHEMES — typically lower-middle-class, religiously motivated, and outside OJK-supervised products; hundreds of illegal entities recorded in the property and land sector. (7) RESIDENTS DISPLACED BY PSN AND MEGA-ESTATE LAND ACQUISITION — fishing and farming communities around PIK 2, Mandalika, Rempang and coastal estates, with weak title and weak bargaining power. (8) BALINESE AND OTHER LOCAL POPULATIONS IN TOURISM PROPERTY HOTSPOTS — priced out of their own land by foreign and Jakarta capital, the most extreme local affordability gap in Indonesia. (9) SANDWICH-GENERATION HOUSEHOLDS — young workers simultaneously supporting parents and attempting to save a down payment, for whom Tapera's 3% deduction is a direct income loss with a distant and uncertain benefit. (10) SMALL AND REGIONAL DEVELOPERS — thinly capitalised firms pulled into subsidised-housing volume targets, who bear the residual risk when land, materials or financing costs move against them.
kasus_china:
CASE 1 — CHINA EVERGRANDE (恒大): the archetype. Peaked as China's largest developer by sales, with more than US$300 billion of total liabilities, over a thousand projects in 280+ cities, and a diversification spree into electric vehicles, bottled water, football and theme parks funded by pre-sale cash. It missed offshore coupons in late 2021, was ordered into liquidation by the Hong Kong High Court in January 2024, saw its founder Xu Jiayin detained, and was delisted in 2025; creditors have warned of an 'uncontrollable collapse' amid 'botched' restructuring. The lesson: a business model in which customer prepayments fund land purchases is a bank without deposit insurance.

CASE 2 — COUNTRY GARDEN (碧桂园): the more instructive case because it was considered the *safe* private developer, concentrated in tier-3/4 cities and family-controlled with a reputation for prudence. It was the largest developer by contracted sales from 2017 to 2022, entered the Fortune Global 500 at #467 with US$23 billion of revenue in 2017, and expanded internationally into Malaysia (Forest City), Australia and Indonesia (Sky House BSD+ and Sky House Alam Sutera+ in Tangerang, ~RMB 1.8 billion / Rp 3.8 trillion). It warned of default in August 2023 and defaulted on offshore debt in October 2023, with ~3,121 pending projects whose fate determines the confidence of buyers in every remaining private developer. The lesson: geographic and reputational conservatism does not protect a business model whose core is leverage against land.

CASE 3 — CHINA VANKE (万科): the slow-motion case still unfolding. The last major developer to have avoided default, majority-influenced by the state-owned Shenzhen Metro Group, repeatedly rescued through shareholder loans, asset sales and — in late 2025 and 2026 — bondholder votes to extend grace periods. Its bond price collapses in November 2025 and its near-default in 2026 revealed that even state backing is conditional, and that the market's 'floor' assumption about SOE-adjacent developers is not guaranteed. The lesson: implicit state guarantees are re-priced when the state's own fiscal capacity is impaired.

CASE 4 — THE HOUSEHOLD SIDE: a buyer in a tier-2 or tier-3 city who purchased in 2021 at peak with a 70-80% LTV mortgage now holds an asset 30-50% below purchase price, is in negative equity, cannot sell into a market with a ~15% foreclosure clearance rate, and is offered interest-only forbearance by a bank that does not want the collateral. Multiply by an estimated 3.3 million homes in negative equity by 2027 and >RMB 200 billion of projected losses. In Zhengzhou at least 500,000 households are reported to have defaulted [uncertain].

CASE 5 — THE FISCAL SIDE: residential land sales revenue down ~65% from its 2020 peak, land revenue at under a third of the 2021 level, and land-use rights having supplied ~40% of local-government income at peak — the mechanism by which a housing correction became a fiscal and then a public-service crisis.

CASE 6 — THE EDUCATION SIDE: Tongji University, the historic pinnacle of Chinese civil engineering, cutting entry scores and still failing to fill its places, while more students applied to transfer out of the major than into it — the clearest single indicator that a society has repriced an entire industry's future.
padanan_indonesia: MEIKARTA (Lippo Cikarang) is Indonesia's Evergrande-in-miniature and its clearest 烂尾楼 analogue: a Rp 278 trillion 'city' announced in 2017 with saturation advertising, sold aggressively off-plan, entangled in a permit-bribery prosecution, delivering only a fraction of promised units, and by 2023 suing its own complaining buyers; by January 2026 the government was proposing to convert parts of it into subsidised rusun. LRT CITY (Adhi Commuter Properti) is the 2025-2026 sequel and the closer parallel to China's mortgage-boycott moment: TOD-branded towers at Ciracas, Tebet and Bekasi topped out but abandoned at the finishing stage from mid-2025, ~2,400 buyers left without units in July 2026, some pursued by debt collectors for KPA instalments, with the Housing Ministry and Danantara brought in — the first time an Indonesian sovereign-fund vehicle has been used to resolve a stranded-buyer crisis. PT HANSON INTERNATIONAL (MYRX) is the landbank-leverage analogue: a claimed ~5,000 hectare landbank (Citra Maja Raya, Forest Hill, Millenium City), unlicensed public fund-raising flagged by OJK in 2019, entanglement in the Jiwasraya and Asabri scandals, and bankruptcy in 2020. THE JAKARTA APARTMENT GLUT is the investor-demand-collapse analogue: >5,000 unsold units, roughly 150 units sold in Jakarta in H1 2025, and secondary prices flat for 2-3 years — a small, contained version of what happened across Chinese tier-3 cities. PIK 2 is the state-designated mega-estate analogue: a ~Rp 40 trillion PSN-designated coastal project by Agung Sedayu/Salim that has generated land-acquisition and sea-fence conflict, structurally echoing the Chinese pattern of state designation plus single-developer land assembly. IKN NUSANTARA is the state-built new-city analogue and Indonesia's clearest ghost-city risk. THE AFFORDABILITY DATA is the human analogue and the most advanced of all: 51% of Gen Z and 40% of millennials unable to buy, only 10% using a KPR, inheritance the dominant route, marriage and home purchase both being deferred — precisely the social pattern China produced a decade earlier. Finally, COUNTRY GARDEN'S SKY HOUSE BSD+ / ALAM SUTERA+ AND CFLD'S TANGERANG PROJECTS are the literal transmission: Indonesian households holding units in projects owned by Chinese developers that have already defaulted or stalled at home.

confidence_level: Sedang-Tinggi (Medium-High). HIGH confidence in: the China macro aggregates (property share of GDP, land revenue collapse, investment/starts/completions declines, NBS price indices, Goldman's demand projections, migrant-worker construction share) — these come from official statistics and top-tier institutions and are mutually corroborating; the developer case histories (Evergrande, Country Garden, Vanke); the Chinese education response (multiple independent outlets, consistent direction and magnitude); the Indonesian structural indicators (mortgage/GDP ~3.4%, IDR 807tn outstanding, IHPR +0.83% YoY, KPR NPL 2.88%, construction 9.82% of GDP, 8.7 million construction workers, FLPP 22.15% execution); and the Indonesian case studies (Meikarta, LRT City, Hanson, Country Garden's Tangerang towers). MEDIUM confidence in: the exact magnitude of China's peak-to-trough price declines (the -30% national and >40-50% city figures come from listing data and commentary rather than an official index, and China's official indices are widely believed to understate declines); negative-equity projections (3.3 million homes by 2027 is a single modelled estimate); the specific -7.6% YoY second-hand figure for October 2025, which is consistent with private 100-city indices but not with the NBS 70-city aggregate; and Indonesian backlog figures, which range from 9.9 million (BPS 2023) to ~15 million (Wamen PKP 2025). LOW confidence in: all forward-looking Indonesian timeline estimates (entry, mainstream, peak years); the lag estimates in years, which are analytical judgements rather than measurements; the Zhengzhou 500,000-default figure; and the Wuhan University architecture-cohort anecdote.
catatan_kontradiksi_data: (1) THE -7.6% YoY SECOND-HAND FIGURE. The research brief cites -7.6% YoY for October 2025, but this cannot be matched to the NBS 70-city aggregate: the NBS October 2025 release shows second-hand YoY indices of 95.3-96.7 for tier-1 cities and worst-case readings of 91.7 (tier-2) and 91.0 (tier-3), while Reuters/Caixin reporting put the December 2025 national second-hand decline at -6.1% YoY. A -7.6% figure is plausible for a private 100-city index (China Index Academy/CRIC) or for a particular tier, and by June 2026 the CIA 100-city readings had reached -6.95% (tier-1), -8.21% (tier-2) and -7.48% (tier-3/4), bracketing -7.6%. Treat the number as directionally correct but index-ambiguous. (2) OFFICIAL VS MARKET PRICE DECLINES. The NBS 70-city index shows cumulative declines of roughly 10-20% from peak, while listing data, brokerage data and market commentary indicate 30-50% in many cities. This gap is systematic, not random: administrative price-drop bans, developer 'gift' incentives that disguise effective discounts, and index-construction choices all bias official data upward. Any analysis relying solely on NBS numbers will understate the crisis; any analysis relying solely on commentary will overstate it. (3) INDONESIAN BACKLOG. BPS 2023 gives 9.9 million units; the Deputy Minister of PKP cited ~15 million households in 2025; industry sources (Majalah REI) explicitly note the absence of an agreed definition (ownership backlog vs occupancy backlog vs habitability). The 3-million-homes programme's target rests on a number nobody agrees on. (4) MORTGAGE/GDP COMPARISONS. The Indonesia ~3.4% figure is current; the comparison set found (Malaysia 31%, India 7%, China 15%) is from 2008 and is not contemporaneous — China's household mortgage stock is now far above 15% of GDP. The direction of the comparison is robust; the specific ratios should not be quoted together. (5) INDONESIAN APARTMENT MARKET NARRATIVE. Sources conflict sharply: some consultancies describe 'stabilisation', 88% occupancy and 'disciplined supply', while Bisnis Indonesia reports >5,000 unsold units and only ~150 Jakarta units sold in H1 2025. The reconciliation is that occupancy (of delivered, largely rented stock) and primary sales (of new stock) are different things; the sales figure is the stress signal. (6) INDONESIAN CIVIL ENGINEERING OUTLOOK. Indonesian career-guidance sources uniformly describe civil engineering as a low-unemployment major with strong prospects, which is currently true given infrastructure spending; this sits in direct tension with the Chinese experience and with the medium-term risk if property development stalls. Both can be true at different horizons. (7) CHINA'S 保交楼 CLAIMS. The 7.5 million completed homes and RMB 7 trillion whitelist figures are state-reported and not independently verifiable; independent researchers (Jamestown, Asia Society) emphasise a persistent policy-reality gap. (8) VANKE'S STATUS. Reporting varies between 'averted default', 'near-default' and 'default risk resurfacing' depending on the date and on whether offshore or onshore instruments are meant; the accurate framing is repeated grace-period extensions rather than a resolution.
